LesionAgent: Training-Free Agentic Tumor Tracking and Response Assessment
in Longitudinal CT

Maximilian Rokuss Affiliation:  Division of Medical Image Computing, German Cancer Research Center (DKFZ), Heidelberg, Germany
Affiliation: Faculty of Mathematics and Computer Science and Email: maximilian.rokuss@dkfz-heidelberg.de    Jeya Maria Jose Valanarasu Affiliation: Medical Faculty, Heidelberg University, Germany  Microsoft Research    Alejandro Lozano    Benjamin Hamm Affiliation:  Division of Medical Image Computing, German Cancer Research Center (DKFZ), Heidelberg, Germany

Affiliation: Faculty of Mathematics and Computer Science and    Fabian Isensee Affiliation:  Division of Medical Image Computing, German Cancer Research Center (DKFZ), Heidelberg, Germany

Abstract

Every few months, a cancer patient’s CT scans decide whether treatment continues. 3D foundation models can now detect, segment, register and track lesions, yet none of them reads the scans as a radiologist does. A radiologist decides which findings are lesions, which are the same lesion months later and whether a new spot means progression, and checks each decision against the extensive rules of a clinical guideline. We introduce LesionAgent, an LLM agent that performs this read end to end without task-specific training. It operates frozen 3D models as tools, acts in 3D through coordinate-labelled views, remembers every lesion across visits in a registry, verifies every model output it relies on, and leaves every number to a deterministic guideline engine. On four public longitudinal CT datasets, LesionAgent tracks more lesions and measures them more accurately than every automatic baseline, and where the same 3D models chained by fixed rules call progression falsely at 33 of 56 follow-ups, it does so twice. On clinical follow-up CTs, it agrees with the radiologists’ response at 20 of 23 follow-ups, including every change in response, and without training on DeepLesion, it retrieves more of its lesions than every tracker trained on it (89.0% vs. 87.4%). Its harness, not its LLM, makes the difference: given the same LLM and 3D models but not the harness, Claude Code reaches a detection F1 of 41% and LesionAgent 78%, and an open-weight LLM that can run inside the hospital rises from 6% to 73%. LesionAgent and a napari reading app for any LLM are available at https://github.com/MIC-DKFZ/LesionAgent.

1 Introduction

Patients with cancer are scanned every few months, and at every scan a radiologist decides whether the disease responds, is stable or progresses. This decision determines whether the treatment is continued, modified or changed. Under the clinical guideline RECIST 1.1 [13], this read means a) finding all lesions in a 3D volume, b) selecting up to five target lesions and measuring them, c) matching each lesion across scans with different fields of view, contrast and anatomy, d) deciding whether a new finding is a new lesion, and e) applying the guideline’s rules. The read is manual and slow, and it varies between readers: two radiologists choose the same target lesions in only 41% of patients [32] and often disagree on the response [27]. Small lesions are easily missed, even by radiologists, whose sensitivity for lung nodules ranges from 51 to 83% [2].

3D foundation models now solve several of these perception steps zero-shot, one at a time. Text-promptable models detect and segment lesions named in natural language [50], promptable models segment them from a click [23], and registration and longitudinal models find a tumor again in a follow-up scan [63, 30, 49]. None of them, however, performs the whole response assessment. It requires composing these models, catching their failures and making decisions no model is trained for: is a finding a lesion, is it the same lesion months later, is a new finding real, and which lesions should be followed? Learning all of this end to end would need longitudinal annotations at a scale that does not exist, as even recent releases cover a single cancer type [33, 30] or a few dozen patients [48].

LLM agents compose pretrained models without training: they call models as tools and solve compositional visual tasks [19, 60, 71], with medical agents calling specialist models for single images or studies [15, 41, 52, 66]. However, none of these agents assesses response across a patient’s CT scans. Current multimodal LLMs cannot take several 3D volumes [17, 59], and even frontier agents that operate a clinical viewer find almost no new lesions in follow-up CT, failing at perception rather than tool use [40, 9]. An agent for this task must act in 3D while it sees only 2D images, remember every lesion across visits over a read of many tool calls, verify model outputs that it can only inspect slice by slice, since a single wrong mask can flip the response, and apply the guideline’s rules exactly.

We introduce LesionAgent, an LLM agent that performs this read end to end, from the CT scans to the response at every visit, without any task-specific training. At baseline, a text-promptable model proposes lesion candidates, and the agent accepts or rejects each one in rendered views. Every accepted lesion enters a registry (lesions ×\times visits) that holds its mask at every visit. The agent chooses the target lesions itself or, if a clinician is available, lets them pick from its best valid sets. At each follow-up, registration carries every lesion into the new scan, where a longitudinal model segments it. If nothing is found, the agent inspects the registered position and records the lesion as absent. A finding that matches no tracked lesion becomes a new lesion only after the agent has checked the same position at baseline. Renders are labelled with voxel coordinates, so the agent turns a position it sees into a 3D tool call, e.g. a click on a lesion that detection missed, and a second model re-segments every mask to catch failures. A deterministic guideline engine measures the lesions on their masks and applies RECIST, so the LLM never computes a number or a category. Another guideline would simply change the engine, not the agent.

We evaluate LesionAgent end to end on four public longitudinal CT datasets, fully automatically or with one click per lesion, with identical settings on every dataset. Since a response is only as reliable as the lesions behind it, we score the detection, tracking and measurement of every lesion as well as the response, against chains of the same 3D models, trained trackers, Claude Code and one-shot LLMs, and against radiologists. Fully automatically, LesionAgent tracks more lesions than every baseline on all four datasets, and where the same 3D models chained by fixed rules call progression falsely at 33 of 56 follow-ups, it does so twice. On clinical follow-up CTs, it agrees with the radiologists’ response at 20 of 23 follow-ups, including all four changes in response (95% balanced accuracy). Its harness, not its LLM, makes the difference: given the same LLM and 3D models on these CTs, Claude Code reaches a detection F1 of 41% and LesionAgent 78%, and an open-weight LLM that can run inside the hospital rises from 6% to 73%. In summary, our contributions are:

  • •

    Training-Free Agentic Tumor Monitoring: LesionAgent is the first agent that reads longitudinal CT end to end, from the images to the RECIST response, using only frozen 3D foundation models. It runs fully automatically or with clinician interaction inside a napari viewer plugin.

  • •

    A Harness for 3D + Time: We let an LLM act in 3D through coordinate-labelled views, remember every lesion across visits in a registry, verify the model outputs it relies on, and leave every number and category to a deterministic guideline engine.

  • •

    Clinically Grounded Reads without Training: LesionAgent agrees with the radiologists’ response on clinical follow-up CTs, measures nodules within their inter-reader variability and retrieves lesions across time better than the trackers trained on DeepLesion. Every response it gives rests on lesions a clinician can check.

2 Related Work

3D foundation models for medical images.

Promptable segmentation has moved from natural images (SAM [31]) to medical adaptations like MedSAM [39], SAM-Med3D [65], SegVol [11] and nnInteractive [23], with text-prompted models such as SAT [74], BiomedParse [73] and VoxTell [50] segmenting structures named in free text. TotalSegmentator [67] remains the standard for organs, and dedicated models segment lesions [10, 49, 64]. Registration models such as ConvexAdam [57] and uniGradICON [63] are used widely to align a patient’s scans across time. However, each of these models solves one step of tumor monitoring.

Longitudinal lesion tracking.

Trackers either predict where a known lesion lies at follow-up or segment it there. Point-based trackers return its position: DLT [4] and TLT [61] retrieve lesion centers on the DeepLesion benchmark [69], and compare against VoxelMorph [3] and DEEDS [20] registration. Volumetric trackers return the lesion’s follow-up mask, segmented after registration [21] or conditioned on the earlier scan [51, 29]. LongiTrack [30] combines a registration-propagated point with the lesion’s baseline appearance to stay robust where single-time-point models degrade because registration displaces the point prompt [47]. All of them follow a lesion that a radiologist has chosen and leave it to the reader which lesions to follow, whether a finding is new and what a change means.

Radiology agents.

Agents that act through tools [71] or write programs over pretrained vision modules [19, 60] answer compositional visual queries without training. In radiology, tool-calling agents select among specialist models across modalities [37], for chest X-ray [15] or for chest CT [41, 52]. In 3D, VoxelPrompt [22] generates code that calls a jointly trained network, multimodal agents call 3D segmentation models [66, 24], and DeepTumorVQA [6] benchmarks tool-augmented agents on CT questions. All of them answer one query about a single study. Current multimodal LLMs cannot take several 3D volumes, so even a longitudinal CT benchmark gives the prior scans as labels [17]. Frontier agents that operate a clinical viewer were shown to find almost no new lesions in follow-up CT [40], with imaging as their hardest domain overall [38, 56]. So far, agents for follow-up imaging assess only brain tumors on MRI: the language model assigns the response category itself [14], or fixed rules score tumor volumes from a segmentation network [25]. To our knowledge, no agent has yet assessed tumor response across longitudinal CT, where many lesions in different organs must be found, matched across scans taken months apart and measured. LesionAgent does so without task-specific training, and every response it gives rests on lesions it has found, tracked and measured itself.

Response assessment and reader variability.

Response criteria turn a patient’s scans into a decision on treatment. RECIST 1.1 [13], the standard for solid tumors in clinical trials, sums the diameters of up to five target lesions and maps their change, together with new lesions, to a response category. Image-based RECIST automation addresses single steps such as diameter measurement [62] or the tracking and measurement of target lesions a reader has selected [8], and language models classify response from the text of the radiologist’s report [42, 36]. In both cases, a radiologist still performs the read. Even between expert readers, this read varies widely: the inter-reader 95% limits of agreement for the change of a single lesion are near ±30%\pm 30\% [72], and readers choose the same target lesions in only 41% of patients [32]. We therefore compare the agent with human readers not only on the final response but also on each step of the read.

3 LesionAgent

Given a patient’s CT scans from several visits, LesionAgent finds, tracks and measures the lesions and assesses the response at every follow-up (Fig. 2). We first define this task, the read, and then describe the agent, its tools and lesion registry, the views through which it acts in 3D, its self-verification and the selection of target lesions.

The read.

A patient study is a series of CT scans s1,…,sTs_{1},\dots,s_{T}, one per visit, with baseline s1s_{1}. At every follow-up, RECIST 1.1 [13] compares the sum of the diameters of up to five target lesions with its baseline value and with its smallest value so far. A decrease of 30% is a partial response and the disappearance of all lesions a complete response. An increase of 20% and 5 mm, a new lesion or clear growth of the other lesions is progression, and everything else is stable disease. The first progression dates the time to progression, a common endpoint of oncology trials.

LesionAgent splits the read by the kind of decision. 3D foundation models perceive the lesions. The LLM judges what the tools cannot, namely whether a finding is a lesion, which lesions are targets and whether a new finding is certainly new, which RECIST calls unequivocal. A deterministic guideline engine computes every number and category.

Agent.

LesionAgent is an LLM in a tool-use loop (Fig. 2). At every step it sees the task and all earlier tool calls with their results, text and rendered images, and chooses the next call. It acts only through 18 typed tools (Tab. 1) on a shared workspace with the scans, the lesion registry, the 3D models and the guideline engine. Without shell, file access or code execution, it cannot change anything outside its read, and with an open-weight LLM on local hardware no image leaves the hospital. A short skill document (Appendix I) describes the reading workflow, the RECIST rules and when to check a result. Claude Opus 5.5 and the open-weight Qwen3.8-27B use it unchanged.

Tools.

detect proposes lesion candidates using VoxTell [50] with multiple prompts, and segment adds a lesion that detection missed, or redoes a wrong tracked mask, from one nnInteractive click [23]. At a follow-up, track_all registers the scans with uniGradICON [63], propagates each lesion’s point and segments the lesion there with LongiTrack [30], its previous mask serving as context. detect then returns only findings that no tracked lesion covers, as candidates for new lesions (all tools in Appendix D).

Lesion registry.

The state of the read lives outside the LLM, in a registry of lesions ×\times visits. Each lesion has a type, an organ, a role (target, non-target, new or rejected) and, at every visit, a mask or a status such as too small to measure, absent or merged with another lesion. Every tool reads and writes the registry, and the report lists every baseline lesion that still lacks a status at a follow-up, so no lesion is silently lost.

Acting in 3D through 2D views.

The LLM sees 2D images, while the tools act in 3D. We therefore label the axes of every view with absolute voxel indices and patient directions, extending coordinate prompting [34, 70] from 2D images to 3D volumes [24]. A position the agent reads off a view can thus become a 3D prompt, e.g. a click on a lesion that detection missed. Every lesion in the registry is outlined in its own colour and labelled with its id at every visit, optionally with its long and short axis, so the agent can tell which lesion it is looking at, compare it across visits and check its measurement. Instead of fixed slices, the agent requests the view that the current decision needs, such as a) slices or a montage through one lesion to check its mask in 3D, b) one lesion side by side at several visits with its registered position to check the tracking, c) a new finding next to the same position at baseline to tell it from a missed baseline lesion, or d) maximum-intensity projections of consecutive 10 mm slabs to find lesions that detection missed, since lung nodules appear there as dots and vessels as lines.

Self-verification.

The 3D models can fail silently. VoxTell masks can be far too small, LongiTrack may follow a neighbouring structure and registration may land next to a lesion (Fig. 4). The tools therefore check every output in code and warn the agent when a check fails. Every VoxTell mask the agent accepts (review_candidates) and every tracked mask gets a second opinion from one nnInteractive click at its centre. If the long axes differ by more than max⁡(5​mm,30%)\max(5\,\mathrm{mm},30\%), about the inter-reader range [72], the agent sees both masks side by side and chooses. A tracked mask is flagged for review across visits (view_pair) if it is empty, changes its volume more than threefold, misses the propagated point, splits or touches another lesion. Since most false new lesions are baseline lesions that detection missed, set_visit_judgement shows every new lesion next to the same position at baseline and lists reasons for doubt, such as a size below 10 mm, no growth or a nearby baseline finding. If any applies, the agent must state why it is certain. Finally, the agent re-checks visits within 5 mm of a response threshold, marked by recist_report, and any progression due to a single new lesion.

Target selection and the guideline engine.

RECIST asks for up to five target lesions, at most two per organ, that are large, represent all involved organs and can be measured reproducibly. Code can check size and these constraints, but reproducibility has to be judged from the images. The agent therefore scores how reliably each measurable baseline lesion can be measured again (qi∈[0,1]q_{i}\in[0,1]), lowering the score for ill-defined margins, necrosis or confluence (score_lesions). Code then enumerates all valid target sets SS and ranks them by the number of organs covered, then by ∑i∈Sqi​si\sum_{i\in S}q_{i}\,s_{i}, with sis_{i} the diameter of lesion ii relative to the largest (propose_targets). The agent takes the best set or justifies another, or lets a clinician choose, e.g. in our napari reading application (Appendix F). The guideline engine measures every lesion on its mask and applies RECIST 1.1 with all its conventions, e.g. short axes for lymph nodes and 5 mm for a target too small to measure. Another guideline, such as iRECIST [55], mRECIST [35], RANO [68] or the Lugano criteria [7], would change the engine, not the agent.

4 Experiments

We evaluate LesionAgent along four axes: (i) the full task end to end, from the images to the response at every visit, against tool chains, specialised trackers, Claude Code and one-shot LLMs; (ii) lesion tracking in isolation against trained trackers; (iii) each step against human readers; and (iv) the contribution of each capability. The agent’s tools are used as released: none of the four longitudinal datasets is in their or the baselines’ training data, nor was any tool trained on DeepLesion tracking. Skill development and all ablations were run on HCUCH.

Data.

All datasets are public (details in Appendix B). HCUCH [48]: clinical RECIST 1.1 target measurements on thorax and abdomen CT of 14 patients with seven cancer types (17 series, 47 scans). TumorMap-Lung [28]: chest CT of 33 lung cancer patients before and during immunotherapy, every lung tumor ≥\geq1 cm contoured and linked across scans. PanTrack [30]: 15 patients (52 visits) with lesions linked over up to 10 visits. NCI-MATCH [12, 26]: CT of 11 patients (23 scans) from the longitudinal subset of the NCI-MATCH trial [16], with lesions contoured and linked across scans. DeepLesion DLS [4]: 960 directed lesion pairs with radiologist RECIST lines at both visits. LIDC-NLST501 [46]: screening CTs, each read independently by four of 20 radiologists.

Settings and baselines.

In the interactive setting, every method gets one click per reference baseline lesion, and in the automatic setting only the images. Interactive baselines are the longitudinal models LesionLocator [49] and LongiTrack [30], and registration followed by the universal lesion segmenter ULS23 [10]. The automatic pipeline chains the agent’s own tools by fixed rules (VoxTell detects, uniGradICON and LongiTrack track, every candidate is accepted). The one-shot LLMs (Qwen3.8 [45], MedGemma 1.5 [18], Opus 5.5 [1]) get all visits in one prompt and answer once (Appendix G). Claude Code runs the agent’s own LLM (Claude Opus 5.5) with a shell and scientific Python on the same images and task. Unlike LesionAgent, which can only call its tools, it may write and run any code. To isolate the harness, we also give it the five 3D models of LesionAgent as Python functions, but not the skill (Tabs. 4 and H). LesionAgent uses the same skill, tools and settings on every dataset. All methods are scored by the same evaluation protocol (Appendix C).

Metrics.

F1: baseline detection of the measurable reference lesions (≥\geq0.5 ml), matched by mask overlap; Rec.: lesion recall on PanTrack and NCI-MATCH, where only some lesions are annotated (PanTrack: the pancreatic tumor) and the response cannot be scored; Track: share of linked reference lesions found again at the next visit (a lesion never found counts as a miss); LD: median absolute long-axis error of the targets against the clinical measurement or reference mask; Resp.: balanced accuracy of the overall response at each follow-up against the reference (Appendix C).

Implementation.

The tools run on one 24 GB GPU. The agent uses Claude Opus 5.5 through the Claude Agent SDK, or Qwen3.8-27B through the same harness. Table 2 reports one read per study. To measure run-to-run variability, we read TumorMap, the largest dataset in Tab. 2, three times (Tab. S3). No clinician answers ask_clinician during evaluation (Appendix F), so the agent decides itself.

5 Results and Discussion

LesionAgent is the strongest method end to end.

Given only the images, LesionAgent tracks more lesions and measures them more accurately than every automatic baseline on all four datasets (Tab. 2). On HCUCH, its detection F1 is 16 points above that of the pipeline built from the same 3D models, at less than half its measurement error. The gains hold across repeated reads, as even the weakest of three TumorMap reads beats every other automatic method in detection, tracking and response (Tab. S3). With one click per lesion, LesionAgent tracks every clinical target on HCUCH and 97% of the NCI-MATCH lesions, where the baselines track at most 84%. Most of the gap between interactive and automatic reads lies in detection, since a lesion that is never found cannot be tracked. Built only from open-weight models, LesionAgent (Qwen3.8) is still the best open method on most metrics, above all the response.

Fixed rules turn model errors into false progressions.

The pipeline runs the same 3D models as LesionAgent, but by fixed rules. Over the 56 follow-ups of HCUCH and TumorMap, it calls progression falsely 33 times, LesionAgent twice (Fig. S1). A fixed rule cannot tell a new lesion from a baseline lesion that detection missed, whereas the agent compares every new finding with the baseline before it records a new lesion.

The agent catches what the models get wrong.

Figure 4 shows one real case per step of a read. Sweeping the lungs slab by slab, the agent adds a nodule that no detector proposed. A second opinion exposes a VoxTell mask that includes a vessel, and the agent’s choice cuts the long-axis error from 9.3 to 1.4 mm. When registration and LongiTrack land on a neighbouring structure without any warning, the agent notices the different anatomy and finds the lesion 30 mm away. A small new spot is not called progression until it has grown at the next scan. The guideline engine then derives the expert’s response at both follow-ups. The agent also knows where it is unsure. For four of its 11 wrong responses on HCUCH and TumorMap, it had asked the clinician about exactly the deciding point. No clinician answers in our automatic evaluation, but in practice one answer would settle such a call (Appendix F).

The harness, not the LLM, makes the difference.

Without 3D models, LLMs do not see the lesions. Given all visits in one prompt, Opus 5.5 finds only 13% of the HCUCH lesions, and Qwen3.8 and MedGemma almost none. Opus still names the response well on HCUCH, where most follow-ups are stable, but its responses rest on lesions it never found, whereas every response of LesionAgent rests on lesions a clinician can check. Claude Code runs the same LLM and may write any code, yet reaches a detection F1 of only 31%. Given the same 3D models as LesionAgent, it tracks and measures as well but still finds far fewer lesions (F1 41 vs. 78%, Tab. 4). In a patient with many lung metastases, it notes them but measures only the two largest liver and six lung lesions, enough for the response. In LesionAgent, every detector candidate stays open in the registry until the agent accepts or rejects it. Inside the harness, even the open-weight Qwen3.8 rises from 6 to 73% F1.

Every part of the harness contributes.

In the ablations on HCUCH (Tab. 4), removing the 3D models halves detection, and replacing the LLM by fixed rules collapses the response. Without the skill, the agent leaves many detector candidates undecided and finds, tracks and measures worse, but still finds more lesions than Claude Code with the same 3D models. Without self-verification, every metric drops. When the LLM assigns the response itself instead of the guideline engine, agreement drops from 95 to 79%, as it counts small spots seen for the first time as new lesions and picks other targets.

Zero-shot tracking beats trained trackers.

To evaluate tracking alone, we use the DeepLesion benchmark (Tab. 4). Without training on it, LesionAgent retrieves 89.0% of the lesions, ahead of TLT (87.4%), the best of the trackers trained on its lesion pairs, and locates them more precisely (mean centre error 4.4 vs. 6.0 mm). These trackers return only a point. Of the trackers that also segment, LongiTrack and LesionLocator return an empty mask for 20 and 37% of the pairs. LesionAgent almost never does and measures the long axis within a median of 2.0 mm of the radiologist. LesionAgent uses the same models as LongiTrack, so the gain comes from what it does when they fail. It compares both visits around the propagated point, searches the overlapping slices and re-segments from a corrected point.

LesionAgent measures like a radiologist but finds fewer lesions.

To compare LesionAgent with radiologists, we add it to LIDC as a fifth reader and score it like each radiologist against the others. It measures nodules of at least 10 mm as accurately as the radiologists and reports fewer false positives, but finds fewer nodules (sensitivity 67 vs. 83%, Fig. 3). On clinical follow-up CT (HCUCH), it agrees with the radiologist’s response at 20 of 23 follow-ups, including all four changes in response, and its time to progression matches in 11 of 12 series. It chooses 17 of the radiologist’s 25 target lesions (Appendix C). For reference, in other cohorts, two radiologists choose different targets in most patients and agree on the response in 74% of cases [32, 27].

Limitations and outlook.

LesionAgent is only as strong as the models it operates. Small lesions, its main gap to radiologists, depend on the detector, and with an open-weight LLM the response still trails the best closed model. Because the harness is model-agnostic, every better detector or open model plugs in without retraining. Public longitudinal cohorts with clinical reads are still small, and HCUCH records only the radiologists’ target lesions, not their non-target or new-lesion calls. Larger cohorts will test more responses and progressions, and a reader study will measure what clinicians add through ask_clinician.

6 Conclusion

We presented LesionAgent, an LLM agent that monitors tumors across longitudinal CT by composing frozen 3D foundation models, remembering every lesion across visits, verifying the models’ outputs in the loop and leaving the final assessment to a deterministic guideline engine. Without task-specific training, it outperforms all automatic baselines end to end, agrees with the radiologists’ response at 20 of 23 clinical follow-ups and retrieves more DeepLesion lesions than every tracker trained on that benchmark. Its harness, not its LLM, makes the difference. Given the same LLM and 3D models, Claude Code reaches a detection F1 of 41% and LesionAgent 78%, and the model-agnostic harness lifts an open-weight LLM from 6 to 73%. Every response it reports is grounded in lesions a clinician can check.

LLM Usage Statement

LLMs are naturally part of the method and of the baselines as this paper is in the realm of agentic AI: LesionAgent runs on Claude Opus 5.5 (Claude Agent SDK) or Qwen3.8-27B, Claude Code runs Claude Opus 5.5, and the one-shot baselines are Qwen3.8-27B, MedGemma 1.5 4B, MedGemma 27B and Claude Opus 5.5 (Sec. 4). We also used Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5) as an assistant to help implement, debug and run code, including the evaluation and plotting scripts, to double-check numbers, and to help draft and edit the text. The authors checked all code, results and text and take full responsibility for the content.

Appendix A Related Methods at a Glance

LesionAgent is, to our knowledge, the first method that performs the whole read on longitudinal CT end to end: from the images alone it finds the lesions, follows them through every visit, measures them, decides whether a follow-up finding is new and assigns the response. Table S1 shows that prior work solves parts of this.

  • •

    Foundation models solve one perception step each and must be told where to look or what to segment: a text prompt (VoxTell), a click (nnInteractive, ULS23), a fixed task (TotalSegmentator) or two scans to align (uniGradICON).

  • •

    Lesion trackers locate a lesion that a reader has found in a follow-up scan [21, 49, 30]. A wrong match stays wrong, and none decides whether a finding is new.

  • •

    RECIST automation measures reader-selected lesions [8] or classifies the response from the radiologist’s report [42]. Our Registration→\toULS baseline follows the first recipe with public models.

  • •

    Medical agents that operate 3D models answer one query about one study [41, 52, 66]. The agents for follow-up imaging assess brain tumors on MRI, letting the language model assign the category [14] or applying fixed rules to volumes from a separate segmentation network [25]. We therefore compare with Claude Code running the same LLM (Appendix H).

LesionAgent operates VoxTell, nnInteractive, uniGradICON, LongiTrack and TotalSegmentator as tools (T in Tab. S1) and adds what they lack: a search for missed lesions, verification of every model output it relies on, a comparison of every candidate new lesion with the baseline, and a deterministic guideline engine for every number and category.

Appendix B Data

  • •

    HCUCH [48] (CC BY 4.0): clinical RECIST 1.1 target measurements by the radiologist. We use the 14 patients (17 thorax or abdomen series, 47 scans) with at least one follow-up. 23 follow-ups have clinical target measurements and form the response reference.

  • •

    TumorMap-Lung [28]: the 33 patients with metastatic non-small cell lung cancer and at least one follow-up, chest CT before and after the start of immunotherapy, with every lung tumor ≥\geq1 cm contoured by two radiation oncologists and labelled consistently across scans.

  • •

    PanTrack [30]: the 15 patients (52 visits) of the official validation split, lesions linked across up to 10 visits. Only the pancreatic tumor is annotated in every scan (liver metastases partly, lymph nodes rarely), so detection is scored as the recall of the pancreatic tumor and the response is not scored.

  • •

    NCI-MATCH [12, 26] (CC BY 4.0): CT from the NCI-MATCH trial [16] with expert contours of at most five lesions per scan and of some new lesions, linked across scans. Of the 18 patients with contoured CT at two or more visits, we use the 11 whose scans cover all contoured lesions at every visit. We checked every link across scans visually and corrected the wrong ones. Due to the partial annotation, detection is scored as recall and the response is not scored.

  • •

    DeepLesion DLS [4]: 480 lesion pairs (960 directed) from 105 patients, each with the radiologist’s RECIST long and short axis at both visits, in sub-volumes of ∼\sim80 mm along zz. These are the official test pairs of the benchmark, on which every method in Tab. 4 is evaluated.

  • •

    LIDC-NLST501 [46]: the 436 of the 501 NLST screening CTs whose patients have a further NLST screening CT on TCIA, each read independently by four of 20 radiologists. We use the scans as single time points for detection and measurement against human readers.

Response references.

Both references apply the RECIST 1.1 rules to expert annotations. HCUCH: the radiologist’s own target lesions and their diameters from the clinical read, per CT series. The reference is the response of these targets (the dataset records no non-target or new-lesion assessment). Thorax and abdomen series of a visit are separate cases because the clinical targets are given per series. TumorMap: the expert tumor segmentations, linked across scans. The targets are chosen by the RECIST rules (the largest measurable baseline tumors, at most two per organ and five in total) and measured on the masks. Tumors that appear only at follow-up are new lesions, and the other baseline tumors are non-targets. None of the four longitudinal datasets is in the training data of the agent’s tools (LongiTrack v1.0 is trained only on AutoPET IV).

Data use and ethics.

All datasets are de-identified and were released by their owners, who obtained the ethics approvals and patient consent, or a waiver of consent, for the original studies. We use them under their licences or data-use agreements, and the owners of TumorMap-Lung confirmed in writing that our use is permitted. No new patient data were collected for this work. LesionAgent is a research system and not validated for clinical use. It can miss small lesions, and a complete-looking report can invite over-reliance, so every response is meant to be checked by a radiologist. The reading application supports this by showing every lesion, measurement and tool call behind the response (Appendix F).

Appendix C Evaluation Protocol

Interactive baselines.

Every interactive method gets one click per reference baseline lesion and uses only its own models. LesionLocator and LongiTrack segment the clicked lesion at baseline themselves and track every follow-up from the baseline (LongiTrack with the click propagated by uniGradICON). Registration→\toULS propagates the click with uniGradICON and segments the lesion at every visit with the ULS23 model.

Fixed rules.

The pipeline and the interactive baselines replace the reader’s judgement by fixed rules: an empty follow-up mask means the lesion has disappeared, and the targets are the best valid set of the same ranking the agent sees (Sec. 3). Only the pipeline searches for new lesions: a follow-up VoxTell candidate ≥\geq10 mm and ≥\geq20 mm away from every baseline finding is a new lesion. The interactive baselines follow the clicked lesions only and report no new lesions.

Metrics.

F1: a reference lesion counts as found if a lesion reported by the method overlaps it. For methods that only measure, the overlap is taken with their calipers (the long- and short-axis lines of a RECIST measurement): a RECIST line drawn across a lesion always overlaps it. Lesions the agent rejected do not count. Detector candidates it left undecided, almost only in the ablation without the skill, have no mask of their own. They count like reported lesions, as found if their centre lies inside a reference lesion and as a false positive otherwise. Recall is computed over measurable reference lesions (≥\geq0.5 ml), precision over all found lesions. PanTrack and NCI-MATCH contour only some lesions per patient. A found lesion outside them can be neither confirmed nor counted as a false positive, so we report the recall alone. TumorMap contours only lung tumors ≥\geq1 cm, so there a found lesion that matches no reference lesion counts as a false positive only from 10 mm long axis, for every method. Track: the share of linked reference lesions that the method’s lesion still overlaps at the follow-up. Lesions never found count as failures. LD: median absolute long-axis error of the targets against the clinical measurement (TumorMap: against the long axis of the matched reference mask at every visit where the lesion is annotated). Resp.: balanced accuracy of the per-visit overall response against the clinical reference (HCUCH) or the mask-derived reference (TumorMap): the agreement is computed per reference category and averaged, so a method that always answers stable disease scores 33%. A visit without a parsable answer counts as wrong. NCI-MATCH is scored like PanTrack, on all contoured lesions (lymph nodes: short axis). In Tab. 2, ±\pm is the standard deviation over 1000 bootstrap resamples of the lesions (Resp.: of the follow-ups).

DeepLesion.

We follow the DLT protocol on all 960 directed pairs: given a lesion’s centre in one sub-volume, predict its centre in the other. We score with the evaluation code released with DLT: CPM@10 counts predictions within min⁡(r,10​mm)\min(r,10\,\mathrm{mm}) of the reference centre (rr: lesion radius), and MED is the mean centre error. For methods that segment, the centre is that of the predicted component (an empty mask falls back to the method’s starting point). Empty is the share of pairs with an empty follow-up mask, and LD the median long-axis error against the radiologist on correctly retrieved lesions. Released methods are run as released, and the agent is run once per pair. No tool was trained to track lesions on DeepLesion: the agent tracks with uniGradICON and LongiTrack (AutoPET IV only).

LIDC fifth reader.

For each radiologist we score detection against the nodules marked by at least two of the other three readers, and the agent against each of these four references (averaged), so that both face the same references. Measurement compares each long axis with the mean of the other readers. The agent read all 436 scans (148 with a nodule ≥\geq10 mm). Reader values are pooled over all reads of the same scans, with 95% CIs from a bootstrap over scans. For nodules ≥\geq10 mm, LesionAgent reaches a sensitivity of 67% [60, 74] against 83% [78, 87] for the readers, with 0.07 [0.05, 0.10] against 0.14 [0.12, 0.18] false positives per scan and a long-axis error of 4.2 [3.5, 4.9] against 4.1 [3.4, 4.9] mm.

Statistics.

Table S2 compares LesionAgent with the strongest baselines at the patient level, and Fig. S1 shows where the response calls of LesionAgent and of the pipeline go.

Run-to-run variability.

A read of the agent is stochastic: single decisions, such as the choice of targets or whether to accept a new lesion, can change the response. To measure this, we read all 33 TumorMap studies, the largest of the four longitudinal datasets, three times with the same code and settings (Tab. S3). Read 1, the first, is the one in Tab. 2. F1 and response vary by 1.5 points (SD) across reads and tracking by 3.5. Of the 33 follow-ups, 26 receive the same response call in all three reads (pairwise Cohen’s κ\kappa 0.76–0.80). Six follow-ups are called wrong in every read, so most wrong calls are systematic rather than chance. Against the other automatic methods, even the weakest read is above all of them in F1, tracking and response, and the long-axis error of the three reads is on par with Claude Code (4.0–4.5 vs. 4.4 mm). Every significant difference on TumorMap in Tab. S2 holds for each of the three reads. We did not repeat the other agentic baselines or Opus one-shot for cost reasons, while the remaining baselines involve no sampling.

Target selection.

The pipeline, which simply takes the best set of our ranking (Sec. 3), already chooses 64% of the radiologist’s target lesions on HCUCH. LesionAgent, which also scores how reproducibly each lesion can be measured and may justify another set, chooses 68%. For reference, two radiologists choose the same target lesions in only 41% of patients [32]. Identical target sets are rare here, because the radiologist distributes up to five targets per patient across thorax and abdomen, while each series is read on its own.

Wrong responses.

Most of the 11 wrong response calls (of 56 follow-ups on HCUCH and TumorMap) lie near a response threshold or follow another target measurement than the reference. LesionAgent misses five of the 11 TumorMap progressions, two of them because it waits for a new lesion to be confirmed at the next scan, which TumorMap does not have.

Appendix D Tool Reference

Table S4 lists the 18 tools by role. They check their outputs in code (Sec. 3) with these thresholds:

  • •

    Second opinion: an nnInteractive click at the mask’s centre disagrees if the long axes differ by more than max⁡(5​mm,30%)\max(5\,\mathrm{mm},30\%). Clicks that leak (>>150 ml) and masks of more than five components are not compared.

  • •

    Tracking: a mask is flagged if it is empty, grows above 3×3\times or shrinks below 0.3×0.3\times its earlier volume, misses the propagated point, splits or touches another lesion.

  • •

    Target choice: the response is recomputed for all near-tied target sets (same organ coverage, score within 15% of the best), naming the lesions whose choice changes it.

Figure S2 compares the fixed pipeline with the agent in three patients. Figure S3 follows six reads of the final agent step by step, in more depth than Fig. 4: the tool calls, what the agent saw, its notes and the result.

Appendix F Interactive Application

LesionAgent ships as a napari [58] plugin that turns the read into a reading application (Fig. S4). A launcher opens a patient’s study and selects the language model, including the open-weight Qwen3.8 on local hardware, so that no image has to leave the hospital. The window shows the read live, as the agent works.

(a) Visit panels. One panel per visit shows every lesion’s outline, in the same colour at every visit, with its registry id and its long and short axis. The panels are linked on the selected lesion: scrolling, panning or zooming one visit moves the others to the same lesion.

(b) Clinician. Each ask_clinician question appears as a card: a yes/no question, a choice between options, or a click on the lesion in a visit panel. The read waits for the answer until a time limit, then the agent decides itself.

(c) Lesion registry. One row per lesion: its site, its role (target, non-target, new), its long ×\times short axis at every visit and its quality flags. Selecting a row focuses all panels on that lesion. The clinician can change a lesion’s role or status, reject it, or ask the agent to re-check it. A right-click in a visit panel segments a lesion at that point. Every change runs through the agent’s own tools, is logged and is reported to the agent at its next turn.

(d) Agent log. The agent’s notes, every tool call with its result and duration, and the renders it saw.

(e) RECIST report. The guideline engine updates it from the registry after every change. For each visit, it shows the sum of target diameters, its change from baseline and from the nadir (the smallest sum so far, from which RECIST measures progression), the target, non-target, new-lesion and overall response, and the distance to the partial-response and progression thresholds. A chart plots the sum over time. Notes flag decisions that need attention, such as a sum within 5 mm of a threshold.

A status panel shows the model that is running, the GPU memory and the tool calls and cost so far. A read can be interrupted and resumed.

Questions during the evaluation.

All results in this paper are fully autonomous reads: nobody answers, and the agent settles every question itself. It asks rarely and to the point: 19 questions in the 50 automatic reads of HCUCH and TumorMap. Almost all concern a decision the response depends on: the choice of targets, a measurement near a response threshold, or whether a finding is tumor or a mimic such as scar or pneumonitis. Many state what is at stake, e.g. “targets #1 and #3 give SD (−-20%), #1 and #16 give PR. Which target set do you prefer?” (SD: stable disease, PR: partial response). The questions find the difficult calls. At four of the 11 follow-ups where the autonomous read disagrees with the reference, the agent had asked about exactly the deciding point. One example is a target sum 0.7 mm below the progression threshold, with the question whether the growing opacity is tumor or radiation pneumonitis. With a clinician in the loop, one answer settles such a call. How much a clinician’s answers improve the read is for a reader study with radiologists to measure, which we leave to future work.

Appendix G One-Shot LLM Baselines: How to Put a Longitudinal CT into an LLM

The one-shot baselines get every visit of a study in one prompt and answer the whole task in one message, without tools. Because the result depends on how a 3D study is shown to an LLM that takes 2D images, we tried the input formats of the literature (Tab. S5). All share the task text, the JSON answer (one box per lesion and visit plus the slice index, converted to calipers through the box centre, along its width and height) and the scoring.

  • •

    Slices: NN axial slices per visit, evenly spaced and labelled with visit and slice index, as in the CT recipe of MedGemma 1.5 [18]. With three visits, 85 slices per visit did not fit MedGemma 1.5 on a 24 GB GPU, so N=40N=40.

  • •

    Encoding: a grey soft-tissue window or MedGemma’s three-window RGB encoding.

  • •

    Video: one video per visit, the input that worked best for Qwen3-VL on a 3D CT benchmark [6, 44].

  • •

    Montage: the agent’s own slab montages with voxel coordinates.

  • •

    Native 3D: NV-Reason-CT [43] reads NIfTI volumes directly.

Single slices beat montages and video for finding lesions. Qwen3.8 with reasoning used up its output budget before answering, MedGemma 1.5 often gave no usable answer for three volumes, and NV-Reason-CT, a report-generation model, never answered in the requested format. Asked only for the response, without finding lesions, the models do no better: Qwen3.8 calls almost every follow-up stable (balanced accuracy 33% on HCUCH, 35% on TumorMap), and MedGemma answers mostly complete or partial response or gives no answer (0–17%).

Appendix H Claude Code Baseline

The Claude Code baseline isolates what the tools add. It is the agent’s model (Claude Opus 5.5, same effort) in Claude Code and gets the same images, days from baseline and RECIST task, but none of the 3D models and not the skill, which describes the tools of LesionAgent. A second run adds the 3D models (Tab. 4). With free code, it can build any analysis it needs, at a higher cost in turns, and so has more freedom than LesionAgent, which acts only through its typed tools. LesionAgent is restricted on purpose: every action is a logged tool call that a clinician can follow, and no generated code runs on patient data.

  • •

    Tools: a shell with Python 3.12 (numpy, scipy, SimpleITK, nibabel, scikit-image, matplotlib, pandas, pillow) and file tools. It renders slices to images and looks at them. No package installs, no limit on turns or time, and in the first run no pretrained model.

  • •

    With the 3D models (Tab. 4): the same setup plus the five 3D models of LesionAgent as Python functions, detect (VoxTell), segment (nnInteractive, from a click or a box), propagate (uniGradICON), track (LongiTrack) and totalseg (TotalSegmentator organs, lung nodules and liver tumors). The models run outside the sandbox and write their masks into its working directory. Its answer may give a mask per lesion and visit, which then serves as the lesion’s segmentation and is measured like the masks of LesionAgent. It gets none of the harness: no view tools, lesion registry, verification, guideline engine or skill.

  • •

    Isolation: it runs in a sandbox in which annotations, our code and our models are not visible, and its working directory holds copies of the scans.

  • •

    Output: the long- and short-axis endpoints of every lesion at every visit on one axial slice, the target lesions, and for each follow-up the non-target status and whether a new lesion appeared.

  • •

    Scoring: as for every method. The guideline engine computes the response from these measurements and judgements (an invalid target set is replaced by the top-ranked valid one), and the caliper lines serve as its lesion masks for F1 and Track (with the 3D models, its own masks where it gives them).

Appendix I The Skill

The skill is a strategy document in plain text that describes the reading workflow, when to verify and the RECIST rules it applies, followed by a RECIST reference and a VoxTell prompt list. It encodes the RECIST 1.1 guideline and general reading practice. Each rule of the RECIST reference names its source in the guideline [13, 53]. All numbers reported for LesionAgent come from one frozen version of the code and the skill, used unchanged for every dataset, model and setting. For the detection-only LIDC and the tracking-only DeepLesion, the task text states what to return. Figures S5 and S6 show the workflow with its main verification and judgement rules. Default prompt lists, display settings, numeric defaults of the tools, minor cases, efficiency hints and the report format are omitted. The full prompt is released with the code.
